Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-02 14:00 PST
Duration: ~48m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Owen (Redwood), Sana (BrightCart CTO), Ethan (Platform Eng), Marta (Sec Ops)
---
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick agenda — triage the 11/30 run where you saw spikes of 5xxs and timeouts, go over the telemetry that Priya pulled, and agree next steps. Sana, do you want to kick us off with how it looked on your side?
[00:22] Sana: yeah, thanks. um so on our side we saw a pretty sharp tail of 502/504s starting around 10:12am, local spike during a cart reprice job. It looked like requests were queuing and then our client-side retry was kicking at 2x, 4x backoff, so we got some doubled traffic. we think some of the large catalog payloads amplified tokenization time.
[00:48] Ethan: adding to that — we saw increased CPU on the app tier and the proxy (we use envoy), which then started returning 502s to clients. we captured traces but not full kv-cache metrics.
[01:10] Priya: yeah, we pulled the Redwood runtime logs. notable things: increased seq length on a subset of requests (some catalog descriptions reached +1.5x tokens), a few long tail kv-cache misses, and a handful of model-side 5xxs that map to the same window. the runtime responded by queuing; after the queue grew past threshold we hit internal timeouts.
[01:36] Marta: from SecOps — we also noticed a burst of auth token refreshes at the same time, so I wonder if SSO churn contributed. we rotate certs at midnight but this is midday, so odd.
[01:50] Jordan: okay — that already suggests three contributing factors: tokenization/seq-length spike, proxy/backpressure, and auth churn. Priya, can you summarize the metrics you captured?
[02:04] Priya: sure. i sent a spreadsheet earlier but quick bullets: median latency during baseline ~120ms, p95 jumped to ~2.3s in the window, p99 to ~6.9s. request rate doubled briefly, concurrency went from 40 to ~180. kv-cache hit rate dropped from 86% to 58% for that job pattern. CPU on model hosts spiked, and a small number of GPUs reported device-level OOM-ish errors (they were not full OOMs, more internal allocator stalls).
[02:38] Jordan: interesting — allocator stalls, not full OOM. Priya, was the model running quantized variants or the default fp16?
[02:45] Priya: this pilot is on a quantized variant but not the aggressive int4— it's a 4/8 mixed quant that we've been using. sometimes quantization regresses headroom and the memory allocator behaves differently under token spikes.
[02:58] Ethan: could that cause 5xxs from the model container or would that be surfaced as higher latency only?
[03:06] Priya: it can be both. if an allocator stall prevents new allocations for kv-cache or attention buffers, the inference engine may return an internal 500 rather than hang forever.
[03:18] Owen: there's also the routing factor — the way the pilot is configured we have a single region with a single capacity pool. when concurrency spiked the scheduler couldn't spill to a fallback region because we pinned to dedicated pool, we should've enabled burst to hosted.
[03:35] Sana: right, we did pin because of data residency concerns; we asked to keep everything in our VPC.
[03:42] Jordan: quick clarification — pinning to the dedicated pool means fallback to hosted can't happen automatically, correct?
[03:49] Priya: correct, unless you allow an explicit failover policy. the platform will honor the VPC isolation.
[03:56] Marta: that falls into our policy requirements — can't move outside VPC without explicit approval. but maybe temporary allowance for burst to a private dedicated pool in same region could be OK. need legal sign-off.
[04:10] Jordan: noted. let's keep that as an option if we need capacity. back to mitigation — Priya, what immediate tuning did you try during the tail?
[04:19] Priya: we throttled incoming concurrency at the router to smooth the load, turned on prefix caching for the most common prompt prefixes (this reduced repeat tokenization work), and temporarily increased the model-side soft-timeout from 6s to 12s for the pilot routes. that reduced 5xx count but increased latency for some callers.
[04:39] Ethan: about the client-side retries — our library retries on 5xx and 429 by default. we use exponential backoff but with a low jitter implementation which might have caused clumping.
[04:52] Jordan: clumping is classic. we recommend randomized jitter and client-side capped retries — 2 retries, with base 250ms and full-jitter stretched.
[05:02] Sana: can Redwood push a small runbook we can embed in our client to reduce retry fan-out?
[05:08] Jordan: yes, I will send that.
[05:12] [05:15] Priya: one more data point — our logs show a couple of rate-limit responses (429) from an internal gateway before the 5xx cascade. so there was a throttle at the front that effectively pushed spikes to the backend.
[05:30] Owen: that suggests the effective service graph had a bottleneck at the API gateway then the model capacity. If the gateway returns 429s, some clients still retry aggressively which then re-enters the system.
[05:43] Marta: would Redwood's automatic prefix/KV caching help if it were pre-warmed?
[05:50] Priya: yes, pre-warming the kv-cache for typical catalog prompts would reduce tokenization time and repeated attention recompute. we can script a prefill using your sample prompt set.
[05:58] Ethan: what's the operational risk of pre-warming? does it consume a lot of memory and cause other evictions?
[06:06] Priya: it consumes memory proportional to the number of cached prefixes; we can size it — e.g., prefilling top 200 prefixes consumed ~2–3GB across the pool in our experiment. that's manageable, but you'd want eviction policies and a small TTL.
[06:22] Jordan: let's map this to immediate next steps — run a 24h controlled replay with variants: (A) current config + improved client jitter, (B) pre-warm top prefixes + smaller batch size, (C) allow temporary burst to same-region hosted pool. Priya will run A/B/C.
[06:38] Priya: note on batch sizing — under high tail concurrency larger batch sizes can reduce throughput latency but increase p99; for your workload with spiky short requests smaller batches helped p95. we'll test 8/16/32 token batch targets.
[06:55] Ethan: is there a recommended default retry behavior for us to adopt server-side or client-side?
[07:00] Jordan: recommend limiting client retries to 2 with full jitter and adding a server-side small queue with clear 429 headers indicating retry-after. avoid blind retries on timeouts; prefer idempotency keys when possible.
[07:14] Sana: on the security front, Marta found a few audit log gaps in the test run — some requests didn't surface redwood session IDs in our SIEM. Marta, can you explain?
[07:24] Marta: yes, some traces had missing session metadata. looked like our proxy was dropping a header during the heavy replay. we need to correlate request IDs across envoy and the Redwood runtime.
[07:36] Priya: we can add an extra trace header injection for the pilot routes to ensure that the runtime emits the same request id. it's a small change but needs coordination with your proxy config.
[07:48] Ethan: we can open a short ICS with our infra team to allow header passthrough for the windowed replay.
[07:55] Jordan: good. any other blockers to running the replay?
[07:58] Sana: we need a clear rollback path in case the replay causes too much production noise. can Redwood throttle quickly?
[08:06] Priya: yes, we can pause or throttle at the routing layer immediately; we also can enable per-route circuit breakers to fail fast to a soft fallback.
[08:14] Owen: also, for the timeouts — increasing the model-side soft-timeout helped but you may prefer graceful degradation via smaller outputs. maybe adjust max_tokens for heavy catalog paths.
[08:26] Ethan: that's acceptable, we can reduce max_tokens for the specific route.
[08:30] [08:32] Jordan: okay quick recap before we schedule the replay window — primary suspected root causes: tokenization spikes increasing seq length, kv-cache misses, gateway 429s causing retry amplification, and VPC pinning preventing quick fallback. mitigations: pre-warm cache, tweak client retry jitter, smaller batch size, temporary burst policy to same-region hosted pool if approved.
[09:00] Priya: i'll run the three replay variants starting tomorrow; we'll capture kv hit rates, p95/p99, internal model 5xxs, allocator stall telemetry, and export those as CSVs.
[09:12] Jordan: Jordan will send the runbook + pricing for burst + recommended client retry snippet by EOD Wednesday (12/03).
[09:20] Ethan: i'll gather envoy/nginx traces and the retry config, and set up the header passthrough change for the replay; due Friday (12/05).
[09:28] Marta: i'll confirm with legal if we can allow temporary failover to same-region hosted pool; if not, we'll rely on other mitigations.
[09:36] Sana: one question — is there any immediate config we should change to reduce the chance of allocator stalls?
[09:42] Priya: short term: reduce per-request max_tokens and lower batch sizes; medium term: we can recommend a slightly different quantization profile with more headroom or configure per-model allocator limits. we'll test the quant variant too in the replay.
[09:58] Owen: from Redwood infra perspective, we can also add a temporary autoscale policy bump for your dedicated pool during the replay window to ensure capacity. that's part of the burst option.
[10:08] Jordan: excellent. last bit — any mention of competitors or alternate approaches we should call out?
[10:14] Sana: we evaluated a managed endpoint from Vendor X but they required broader data egress; not an option. thank you.
[10:20] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll reconvene after the replay results — propose Friday 12/05 at same time to review.
[10:28] Ethan: works for me.
[10:30] Priya: thanks, I'll post the raw CSVs and a short notes doc to the shared drive.
[10:36] Jordan: great — meeting adjourned.
